newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Independent central banks sprout globally.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Independent central banks sprout globally.

text.p: Independent central banks are springing up across the globe, but recent rows in Europe show how fragile independence can be and tension persists between central banks and their political masters.
The power of financial markets to punish countries with policies deemed excessive has convinced governments from Nepal to Britain that central banks should be granted independence.
But independence comes in degrees and politicians only surrender their power grudgingly, central bankers admit.
"Independence is like a red flag to finance ministries so many central bankers don't like to use the word," one commented.
In return for independence, central banks now receive specific mandates and are held accountable for their actions.
The German Bundesbank model of independence is rare and waning.
"In the old days central banks set their own targets," said one central banker, referring to the Bundesbank.
"Now it is much more common for governments to supply central banks with mandates for price stability, which are then explicitly defined as an inflation target," he added.
Independent central banks are today defined by the extent of their power, their mandates, accountability and transparency.
"In a democracy there is no such thing as complete independence for central banks and of course governments have to be involved," said a North American central banker.
The balance of power may currently favour central banks over governments, but these unelected officials are well aware that their independence ultimately rests on public support.
This support must be continuously earned to ensure backing for policy measures that can be harsh and unpopular.
"In other words a central bank only has the independence that it deserves," Swiss National Bank (SNB) chairman Hans Meyer said in a speech last month.
THE BIRTH OF INDEPENDENT CENTRAL BANKS
The origin of central banks stems from government's monopoly to issue bank notes. But notes printed by central banks had to be credible to fulfil their function as a means of payment.
Credibility was only earned slowly. Many a central bank misused its power as a banker to the government and freely issued notes so governments could finance their spending.
But public opinion shifted during the inflationary 1970s when it was realised that only central banks with some form of independence could resist political pressures.

"The experience of the 1970s and early 1980s increased the awareness of the cost of inflation, and there was a danger of inflation from central banks that were subject to political bodies," said one European central banker.
At the start of the 1980s only Germany, Switzerland and the United States, among the major financial powers, had independent central banks.
But the tide turned. Independence from political meddling is now viewed as a prerequisite for a credible monetary policy.
"Independence became a way of protecting against inflation," said one central banker.
The victory of the Bundesbank in its dispute with the Bonn government over gold revaluation not only illustrated the popular support it enjoys but enhanced its credibility.
Meeting the Maastricht criteria through creative accounting was frowned on by the German public and reinforced many people's dim view of politicians.
Once the European Union (EU) decided in favour of an independent central bank, any potential future member -- either in Western or Eastern Europe -- had to adopt the principle.
STEPS TO BOOST CREDIBILITY
Along with growing independence, central banks have also become more transparent and sought to boost their credibility.
Information is the essential component of markets and central banks have improved their transparency as they seek to work with and not against financial markets.
"Markets could not be told what to do, they had to be given good reasons for doing it," the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said in its 1996/97 annual report.
This shift toward greater transparency is best illustrated by the increased use of explicit inflation targets, for example by New Zealand or Britain.
But transparency rests on credibile information and credibility can only be gained over time.
In the late 1980s German interest rates were below those of France, partly because of the credibility attached to the anti-inflationary zeal of the Bundesbank.
With transparency comes accountability. Having granted central banks independence to pursue certain mandates, governments then judge their efficiency.
In Japan, for example, the new laws giving independence to the Bank of Japan (BOJ) also obligate it to submit a report to parliament every six months.
RECENT DEVELOPMENTS IN CENTRAL BANK AUTONOMY

-- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) will be given independence from the Ministry of Finance. The government will only be able to ask the BOJ's policy-making board to postpone a decision, while now it can order the BOJ to do so. Transparency at the BOJ will also be improved and the bank will submit a report to the Japanese parliament every six months.
-- The Bank of Lithuania is drawing up a new law so it will meet EU regulations for independence. The bank will no longer be permitted to extend credit to the government.

-- Sweden has proposed a law that prohibits all authorities from giving instructions to the Riksbank on monetary policy and establishes price stability as the bank's primary objective. The governor's position will also be strengthened and a new board, with responsibility for monetary decisions, will be created.
-- Romania is preparing a new law that lays down price and currency stability as the main tasks of the central bank.

-- The Bank of Israel has proposed a board to oversee monetary policy and make price stability the main goal. Accountability and transparency will also be improved. Government can still set the inflation target but will leave implementation to the bank.
-- Cuba has set up a new central bank which is autonomous and is a separate legal entity. Although carrying out government policy, it will regulate monetary and credit policy.
-- The Greek government has submitted a draft law to parliament that would increase the independence of the central bank.
-- Nepal plans to grant its central bank full independence from the Finance Ministry, which currently supervises the bank.
-- The new Polish constitution gives the central bank independence from parliament and government in setting and pursuing monetary policy goals and establishes a monetary policy council.
-- Taiwan is considering giving its central bank independence in monetary policy, with price stability as its top priority.
-- The British government now allows the Bank of England to set interest rates, but government sets the inflation target. A monetary policy committee has been created.
-- South Korea is planning financial reform that includes increased Bank of Korea independence, but also responsibility for meeting targets.
-- The Swiss National Bank (SNB) wants a revised Swiss constitution to fix price stability as its main objective.
